newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit new high, bonds rise, dollar weaker.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit new high, bonds rise, dollar weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rebounded from a sharp sell-off to close at a record high Monday as bonds staged a recovery ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting Tuesday.
The dollar, however, remained weaker after falling with the stock and bond markets.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 6.28 points at 5,894.74, which surpassed last Monday's record close of 5,889.20. Early in the day, the index was off 53 points due to weakness in bonds.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,425 to 863 on moderate volume of 297 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"We're just seeing statistical noise in anticipation of the Fed meeting tomorrow," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon & Farrell.
"There were some nervous Nellies selling stock at the open and then this afternoon we had bargain-hunters," he said.

Wall Street focused on Tuesday's meeting of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee. The speculation is that it could bump up short-term interest rates by one quarter or one half of a percentage point to ward off inflationary pressures.
There is also the possibility that the FOMC may do nothing and leave interest rates unchanged ahead of the November elections.
The concern is that a rise in interest rates could slow the growth of corporate profits and consumer spending.
The Fed last moved on interest rates by cutting the rates by one quarter percentage point on Jan. 31.

The bond market erased losses in the afternoon on a Reuter report quoting an unidentified Fed source that the Fed was set on achieving long-term price stability and was close to adopting a core Consumer Price Index target as the basis for monetary policy. The core CPI excludes volatile food and energy prices.
The report reassured Wall Street that the central bank remained vigilant in its inflation fight -- good news for stock investors who are afraid that inflation could eat away at their investments.
The source said the Fed views a zero to 2 percent range on core CPI as price stability. The core is currently at 2.6 percent on an annualized basis.
The key 30-year Treasury bond jumped a quarter point, lowering its yield to 7.02 percent from 7.04 percent at Friday's close.
Only a handful of economists expect the Fed to bump up interest rates by one half of a percentage point -- an aggressive move that would unnerve the stock market.
In late New York trading, the dollar stood at 1.5125 German marks and 109.89 Japanese yen, down from 1.5160 and 109.96 late Friday.

November soybeans at the Chicago Board of Trade closed up 3-1/2 cents a bushel at $7.98-3/4 as forecasts for frost this week in the U.S. Midwest deepened concerns that cold weather had already hurt maturing plants.
December corn closed down 1 cent per bushel at $3.13-1/4.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed 44.4 points lower at 3,919.7, after climbing to a record 3,994.1 on Friday. Tokyo's stock market was closed for a national holiday.
